Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 47
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Plumber
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by caregiver (childhood)
  pcl5: 62

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Auditory (Sounds): Related sounds, Name Reminders: Hearing related names, Auditory (Voice): Related voice
  Maladaptive Strategies: Other-Blame Rumination: I dwell on what other people have done to me, Avoid Authority Figures: Being around people in authority or uniform, Avoid Perpetrator Cues: Anything that reminds me of the person who harmed me
  Negative Appraisals: Character Blame: The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am, Lost Meaning: Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore, Defective Self: There is something wrong with me as a person

Vignette:
Akua had always been skilled with her hands, able to fix just about anything that was broken. As a plumber, she took pride in being able to provide for her family and keep their home running smoothly. But despite her competence, Akua couldn't shake the feeling that she was somehow broken herself. It started when she was just a child, living with her mother's boyfriend who would often lash out at her physically. The sound of his voice, low and menacing, still sent shivers down her spine. She remembered one particularly brutal beating, where he had slammed her against the wall, leaving her with a deep gash on her forehead. The sound of his footsteps, heavy and deliberate, as he approached her, was forever seared into her memory. As she grew older, Akua began to realize that certain sounds could transport her back to those terrifying moments. The clang of pipes in the walls, the rumble of thunder outside – anything that reminded her of her abuser's voice or movements would send her spiraling into a panic. She found herself avoiding places where she might hear such sounds, like construction sites or even her own workshop at times. Akua also struggled with hearing certain names, particularly those that sounded similar to her abuser's. A coworker mentioning someone named "Kevin" in conversation would make Akua's heart skip a beat, as if Kevin himself was standing right behind her. She tried to brush it off as mere coincidence, but deep down, she knew it was more than that. Her avoidance behaviors extended beyond just sounds and names, too. Akua found herself becoming increasingly wary of authority figures – police officers, bosses, even doctors. There was something about their uniforms or air of confidence that made her feel small and powerless all over again. She began to limit her interactions with such individuals, often going out of her way to avoid them altogether. Akua's ruminations on the abuse she suffered also consumed a significant portion of her mental energy. She couldn't help but replay the events in her mind, wondering what she had done to deserve such treatment. The thought that it was somehow her fault – that there was something fundamentally wrong with her as a person – haunted her daily. Her sense of self-worth began to erode, leaving her feeling like nothing more than a defective, unfixable thing. As time went on, Akua noticed that her relationships suffered as well. She became increasingly withdrawn and isolated, pushing away even those closest to her. Her husband, trying his best to be supportive, would ask her what was wrong, but Akua just couldn't seem to articulate the pain and fear that had taken up residence inside her. One day, after a particularly grueling project at work, Akua broke down in tears in front of her coworker. It was then that she realized she needed help – not just for herself, but for those around her who were suffering alongside her. The thought of facing her demons head-on terrified her, but Akua knew it was the only way to reclaim some semblance of meaning and purpose in her life. As she sat in her therapist's office, Akua finally began to confront the traumas of her past. With each passing session, she slowly started to unravel the tangled web of negative appraisals that had held her captive for so long. Though it was a daunting journey ahead, Akua felt a glimmer of hope – perhaps, just perhaps, she wasn't as broken as she thought, and that with time and effort, she could learn to mend herself after all.
